topic: The Geometry of Linear Transformations: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
target_audience: University students (Undergraduate level, introductory Linear Algebra)

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Transformation View
sections.content: Briefly define a linear transformation as a stretching/rotating grid. Visualize a vector 'v' moving to 'Av'. Most vectors change direction during this transformation.
sections.example: Visualize a grid of square tiles being sheared and stretched by a matrix A.

sections.title: Defining Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues
sections.content: Introduce the 'staying put' concept: Eigenvectors are special vectors that do not change direction when the transformation is applied; they only scale by a factor λ (the eigenvalue). Formula: Av = λv.
sections.example: A spinning globe: The axis of rotation is the eigenvector (it doesn't move), and the eigenvalue represents the rotation speed/scale factor.

sections.title: Visualizing the Concept
sections.content: Use a graphical animation showing a 2D plane. Show a vector rotating, then highlight the 'lucky' vectors that remain on their original span line while stretching or shrinking.
sections.example: A vector pointing from the center of a clock to the number 3, which stays pointing at 3 even if the clock face is stretched horizontally.

sections.title: Constructing an Eigenbasis
sections.content: Explain that if we find enough linearly independent eigenvectors, they form a new coordinate system—an 'eigenbasis'. In this basis, the complex transformation matrix becomes a simple diagonal matrix.
sections.example: A character navigating a maze: Instead of using North/South coordinates (standard basis), they use the 'Eigen-directions' (the paths of least resistance), making the math of their movement trivial.

sections.title: Real-World Application Summary
sections.content: Briefly connect the theory to real-world impact: Stability analysis, image compression (PCA), and quantum mechanics.
sections.example: A search engine algorithm using eigenvectors to rank the importance of 'nodes' (webpages) in a giant network.
